title: Nominalisation and academic style
tagline: Turn the verb into a noun and the sentence gains the weight of a report.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 3 — word formation (noun-forming suffixes)
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (verb/adjective → noun phrase)
Writing Part 1 — essay: an impersonal, formal register
Writing Part 2 — report: findings built around abstract nouns rather than personal verbs
why: Nominalisation — turning a verb or adjective into a noun — is the single biggest difference between a sentence that sounds spoken and one that sounds written. 'The company failed because managers decided badly' becomes 'The company's failure was due to poor management decisions': the same information, restructured around nouns instead of verbs. C1 Advanced tests the noun-forming suffixes directly in Use of English Part 3 and rewards the technique in the essay and report — but a whole paragraph built only from nominalisations sounds stiff, so knowing when not to use it matters just as much.

diagrams.title: From verb sentence to noun phrase

before.text: The government decided to raise taxes suddenly, and this surprised everyone.

after.text: The government's sudden decision to raise taxes surprised everyone.

steps: Turn the main verb into its noun form: decided → decision.
Attach the subject as a possessive or an of-phrase: the government's decision.
Fold adverbs into adjectives before the noun: 'decided suddenly' → 'sudden decision'.

diagrams.title: How do verbs and adjectives become nouns?

rows.label: Verb
cells: a full verb carrying the action: decided, failed, improved
a 'light' verb + noun: made a decision, resulted in failure

rows.label: Risk
cells: can sound too informal for a formal essay
overused, it sounds abstract and hard to follow

head: Base word
Suffix
Example
rows: The committee's decision will be announced on Friday.
There is a strong likelihood of rain this weekend.
The failure of the crop led to a sharp rise in prices.
Public awareness of the issue has grown steadily.
The difference between the two proposals is significant.
Her argument rests on three pieces of evidence.

use.point: Compressing a clause into a noun phrase with pre- and post-modification

examples.text: The sudden collapse of the bridge forced the council to close the road.
examples.note: adjective + noun + of-phrase replaces 'the bridge suddenly collapsed'

examples.text: Growing concern about air quality has pushed the city to act.
The report examines the likelihood of further delays.
examples.note: likely → likelihood, followed by an of-phrase

use.point: Abstract nouns with 'the + noun + of' for formal, impersonal writing

examples.text: The introduction of the new syllabus was met with mixed reactions.
examples.note: the verb 'introduce' nominalised; the agent is not named

examples.text: The reduction in traffic during the holidays is well documented.
The lack of clear guidelines caused confusion among staff.
examples.note: a nominal phrase avoids naming who lacked the guidelines

use.point: Impersonal subjects that hide the agent

examples.text: Concerns have been raised about the reliability of the data.
examples.note: impersonal — nobody is named as the one worrying

examples.text: An improvement in exam results was observed after the new timetable began.
examples.note: nominalisation plus a passive removes the agent completely

examples.text: The assumption that costs would fall proved wrong.
examples.note: assume → assumption, used as an impersonal subject

examples.text: Miss Vega explained the theory clearly — not 'Miss Vega gave an explanation of the theory'.
examples.note: in speech and narrative, the verb form is more natural

examples.text: We decided to leave early — not 'we made the decision to leave early'.
The instructions simply say 'Submit your essay by Friday' — not 'submission of your essay is required'.
examples.note: direct instructions and requests stay verbal

watch_out.wrong: The likely of rain is high.
watch_out.why: 'Likely' is an adjective; the noun form is 'likelihood', not 'likely'.

watch_out.wrong: There was a big improve in her writing.
watch_out.right: There was a big improvement in her writing.
watch_out.why: The noun form of 'improve' is 'improvement', not the bare verb.

watch_out.wrong: The success of the plan depend on funding.
watch_out.right: The success of the plan depends on funding.
watch_out.why: Once the verb becomes a noun, the following verb must agree with the new singular subject: success depends, not depend.

watch_out.wrong: The teacher gave an explanation the theory.
watch_out.right: The teacher gave an explanation of the theory.
watch_out.why: A nominalised verb keeps its usual preposition (explain something → an explanation of something); it cannot take a direct object.

watch_out.wrong: The city made an announcement of new the rules.
watch_out.right: The city made an announcement of the new rules.
watch_out.why: Word order inside the noun phrase follows normal English order: article + adjective + noun.

watch_out.wrong: Please do a submission of your homework by Friday.
watch_out.why: A simple instruction is clearer as a verb; overusing nominalisation in direct requests sounds unnatural and bureaucratic.

dialogue.title: From chat to essay
dialogue.context: Miss Vega is helping Nadia and Liam turn a spoken-sounding paragraph about plastic waste into formal essay style for their Writing Part 1 practice.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Read your first sentence — it needs to sound like an essay, not a conversation.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: 'The factory polluted the river and people got really angry.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good content, informal style. Can you turn 'polluted' into a noun?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: 'The factory's pollution of the river provoked anger among local residents.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Much better. Liam, what about your sentence on recycling?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I wrote: 'The city introduced a new law and now people recycle more.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Try building it around the introduction of and an increase in.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: 'The introduction of the new law has led to an increase in recycling rates.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Exactly. But be careful — don't nominalise every single verb, or the paragraph turns stiff.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: So for the conclusion, should I still write 'We recommend that the city acts now', not 'Our recommendation is action'?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Yes — a direct recommendation like that reads better as a verb. Save the noun style for the body paragraphs.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: So it's a balance: the reduction of plastic waste in the introduction, but 'we should act' in the conclusion.

items.sentence: The ___ of the negotiations took everyone by surprise.
There is a strong ___ that the match will be postponed because of the rain.
items.why: the noun form of 'likely' is 'likelihood', an irregular -hood suffix, not 'likeliness'

items.sentence: Her sudden ___ to resign surprised the whole team.
The government's ___ of the new policy faced strong opposition.
Growing public ___ about climate change has changed consumer habits.
The ___ between the two reports is hard to explain.
Please ___ your assignment by Friday, not 'make a submission of'.
items.why: a direct instruction is clearer as a verb — avoid unnecessary nominalisation

items.sentence: The team's ___ in the final was celebrated across the school.
items.why: succeed → success, an irregular noun form

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct noun form of the word in brackets.

items.sentence: The ___ (fail) of the first attempt taught the team a great deal.
There is little ___ (likely) of snow this far south.
The committee reached its ___ (decide) after a three-hour meeting.
The gradual ___ (improve) in air quality has been widely reported.
Public ___ (aware) of the campaign grew within days.
The unexpected ___ (arrive) of the inspector caused panic in the office.
Her ___ (argue) convinced even the sceptics on the panel.
The school's ___ (achieve) in the regional science fair was widely praised.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. The answer should be a noun phrase built from the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: The negotiations failed, and this surprised no one.
Her writing improved significantly over the term.
items.second_end: in her writing over the term.

items.first: The team achieved a remarkable result this year.
The government announced new tax rules, and this worried many small businesses.
items.second_end: of new tax rules worried many small businesses.

items.first: People are becoming more aware of plastic pollution, and this is changing shopping habits.
items.second_end: of plastic pollution is changing shopping habits.

items.first: The course requires a great deal of independent study.
items.second_end: for independent study on this course is considerable.

summary: Turn the verb or adjective into its noun form (decide → decision, aware → awareness, likely → likelihood) and attach the subject as a possessive or an of-phrase.
Watch the suffix families — -tion/-sion, -ment, -ity, -ness, -ance/-ence — and the irregular nouns that follow none of them (fail → failure, succeed → success).
Fold adverbs into adjectives before the noun: 'decided suddenly' becomes a sudden decision, not 'a suddenly decision'.
Nominalisation removes the agent and suits reports, essays and academic writing — but a whole paragraph of noun phrases sounds stiff.
Keep instructions, conclusions and direct recommendations verbal: submit your work, not the submission of your work is required.
